## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of namespace isolation and basic egress filtering using NetworkPolicy. It checks hands-on ability to craft minimal, enforceable rules and verify them.

## Key Concepts
- Kubernetes NetworkPolicy basics
- Namespace-scoped isolation
- Egress rules and default deny
- Basic verification via kubectl and logs

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: test-egress-isolate
  namespace: test
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.1.2.3/32
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {}
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
        except:
        - 255.255.255.255/32
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53
```

```yaml
# Compliant Pod in test namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: compliant-pod
  namespace: test
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 300"]
```

```yaml
# Noncompliant Pod in test namespace (tries to access prod)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: noncompliant-pod
  namespace: test
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "wget http://prod.svc.cluster.local || true"]
```

```yaml
# DNS test Pod (for compliance with DNS allow rule)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: dns-test
  namespace: test
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local"]
```

- Check events: kubectl describe networkpolicy/test-egress-isolate -n test

## Why This Is Asked

Deprecations pose production risk in multi-tenant clusters. This question probes practical policy design across CI and runtime using Gatekeeper and Kyverno, plus concrete manifests and validation strategy.

## Key Concepts

- Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
- Kyverno admission policies
- Kubernetes API deprecations and upgrade paths
- CI validation with kubeconform/kubeval
- Runtime admission controls and auditability

## Code Example

```yaml
# Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate (simplified)
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8sdeprecatedapi
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sDeprecatedAPI
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8sdeprecatedapi
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        deprecated := ["apps/v1beta1", "networking.k8s.io/v1beta1"]
        api := input.review.object.apiVersion
        api == deprecated[_]
        msg := sprintf("deprecated apiVersion used: %v", [api])
      }
```

```yaml
kind: Deployment
metadata:

      containers:
      - name: app
        image: example/old:1
```

```yaml

kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: new-deploy
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: example/new:1
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests foundational secure supply chain practices in a beginner-friendly manner. It mirrors real-world CI gates used in production environments around Dockerfile hygiene, image signing, SBOM generation, and registry controls. It introduces modern tools like Cosign and SBOM attestations without overwhelming complexity.

## Key Concepts

- **Dockerfile Hygiene**: Non-root USER and multi-stage builds reduce security vulnerabilities and image size
- **Container Image Signing**: Using Cosign to sign and verify container images ensures integrity
- **SBOM Attestation**: Software Bill of Materials provides transparency into image contents and dependencies
- **GitHub Actions Workflows**: Implementing gates and policy checks in CI/CD pipelines
- **Registry Allowlist**: Restricting deployments to approved registries prevents supply chain attacks

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal GitHub Actions workflow
name: Docker Security Gate
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Validate Dockerfile
        run: |
          # Check for non-root USER
          grep -q 'USER ' Dockerfile || exit 1
          # Check for multi-stage build
          grep -q 'FROM.*AS' Dockerfile || exit 1
      
      - name: Build and push image
        run: |
          docker build -t ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker push ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: |
          syft ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }} -o spdx-json > sbom.json
      
      - name: Sign image and SBOM with Cosign
        run: |
          cosign sign ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
          cosign attest --type spdx-json --predicate sbom.json ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Verify signature and attestation
        run: |
          cosign verify ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question demonstrates end-to-end supply chain security expertise: image signing, SBOM provenance tracking, CVE scanning, and runtime verification in a multi-cloud, high-stakes environment. It tests knowledge of Sigstore ecosystem tools and policy enforcement.

- Image signing with Cosign/Sigstore for supply chain integrity
- CycloneDX SBOM generation for component transparency
- CVE scanning integration (e.g., Trivy, Snyk) for vulnerability detection
- Gatekeeper/OPA policy for runtime enforcement
- Canary deployments and rollback strategies in multi-cloud contexts

## Code Example

### GitHub Actions Workflow (`.github/workflows/ci.yaml`)
```yaml
name: Image Provenance Gate
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  build-scan-sign:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Build and push image
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/org/app:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker push ghcr.io/org/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Generate CycloneDX SBOM
        uses: cyclonedx/ghcr-create-sbom@v1
        with:
          format: json
          output-file: sbom.json
      
      - name: Run CVE scan
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          image-ref: 'ghcr.io/org/app:${{ github.sha }}'
          format: json
          exit-code: '1'
          severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH'
      
      - name: Sign image with Cosign
        uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@v3
        with:
          cosign-version: 'v2'
      - name: Sign image
        run: |
          cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/org/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Generate SBOM with Syft
        run: |
          syft ghcr.io/org/app:${{ github.sha }} -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
```

### Gatekeeper Policy (`constraint-template.yaml`)
```yaml
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: requirecosignsignature
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: RequireCosignSignature
      targets:
        - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
          rego: |
            package requirecosignsignature
            violation["image is not signed with Cosign"] {
              image := input.review.object.spec.containers[_].image
              notcosign.verify(image)
            }
```

### Failing Manifest (Unsigned Image)
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: unsigned-app
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: ghcr.io/org/app:unsigned-latest
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8080
```

### Passing Manifest (Signed Image)
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: signed-app
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: ghcr.io/org/app:v1.0.0
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8080
```

### Verification Steps
```bash
# Verify image signature
cosign verify ghcr.io/org/app:v1.0.0

# Verify SBOM exists
cosign verify-attestation --type cyclonedx ghcr.io/org/app:v1.0.0

# Verify against Gatekeeper policy
kubectl get requirecosignsignature
```

```yaml
# Istio AuthorizationPolicy (compliant example)
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: mongodb-per-tenant-access
  namespace: tenantA
spec:

  - from:

    to:
    - operation:
        ports: ["27017"]
```

```yaml
# Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate (pseudo)
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8sspiffe
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: SPIFFEIsTenantScoped
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8sspiffe
```

## Why This Is Asked
This question rigorously tests practical CI security knowledge for multi-tenant infrastructure, covering both container images and WASM modules deployed across edge and cloud environments. It evaluates understanding of supply chain security, provenance verification, and admission control policies.

- **Manifest Validation**: Ensuring Kubernetes manifests reference only cryptographically verified signed artifacts
- **Admission Control**: Kyverno or OPA policies for runtime enforcement in Kubernetes clusters
- **GitHub Actions**: CI/CD workflow implementation for automated security gates

## Implementation Overview
The solution requires:
1. Cosign key pair management with public key distributed across CI/CD and cluster admission controllers
2. SBOM generation during build (using tools like Syft or SPDX)
3. Rekor integration for attestation verification
4. Policy engine (Kyverno/OPA) to validate signed references at admission time
5. Local developer verification scripts using cosign CLI

## Why This Is Asked
This task tests practical CI gating for container hygiene: linting with Hadolint and enforcing image tagging discipline across manifests.

## Key Concepts
- Hadolint integration in GitHub Actions
- YAML parsing to inspect image tags
- Regular expressions for pinning (no latest, no -dev) and clear failure messages
- Practical debugging of lint vs. policy failures

## Code Example
```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci-docker-k8s.yml
name: CI Gate: Dockerfile lint + tag pin
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, master ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ '**' ]
jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hadolint/hadolint-action@v3
        with:
          dockerfile: '**/Dockerfile'
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question evaluates the ability to encode security baselines as policy-as-code and enforce them in CI/CD pipelines for multi-tenant clusters. It tests understanding of threat modeling, policy granularity, and how to allow exceptions in a controlled manner.

## Key Concepts

- **Open Policy Agent (OPA) with Rego**: Declarative policy language for Kubernetes admission control
- **Pod Security Standards**: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, privilege escalation, and security profiles
- **Volume Security**: hostPath, hostNetwork, and hostPID considerations in multi-tenant environments

## Rego Policy

```rego
package kubernetes.admission

deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
  container.securityContext.runAsNonRoot != true
  msg := "Containers must run as non-root (runAsNonRoot: true)"
}

deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
  container.securityContext.privileged == true
  msg := "Privileged containers are not allowed"
}

deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
  container.securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem != true
  msg := "Containers must use readOnlyRootFilesystem"
}

deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  input.request.object.spec.hostNetwork == true
  msg := "hostNetwork is not allowed"
}

deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  input.request.object.spec.hostPID == true
  msg := "hostPID is not allowed"
}

deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  volume := input.request.object.spec.volumes[_]
  volume.hostPath
  not allowed_hostpath[volume.hostPath.path]
  msg := sprintf("hostPath volume %s is not allowed", [volume.hostPath.path])
}

allowed_hostpath {
  input.request.namespace == "kube-system"
}

allowed_hostpath[path] {
  allowed_paths := [""]
  path := allowed_paths[_]
}
```

## Failing Manifest

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: insecure-pod
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:latest
    securityContext:
      runAsNonRoot: false
      privileged: true
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: false
  hostNetwork: true
  hostPID: true
  volumes:
  - name: data
    hostPath:
      path: /var/data
```

## Passing Manifest

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secure-pod
  namespace: production
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:stable
    securityContext:
      runAsNonRoot: true
      privileged: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      seccompProfile:
        type: RuntimeDefault
  securityContext:
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  volumes:
  - name: cache
    emptyDir: {}
```

## CI Verification Steps

1. **Install OPA CLI**: `brew install opa` or download from https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/
2. **Test Rego policy**: `opa eval --format pretty --data policy.rego --input failing-pod.json "data.kubernetes.admission.deny"`
3. **Verify failing manifest**: Should return denial messages for each violated policy
4. **Verify passing manifest**: Should return empty deny array
5. **CI/CD Integration**: Add OPA gate to your pipeline:
   ```yaml
   # GitHub Actions example
   - name: Run OPA Gate
     run: |
       opa eval --format json --data policy.rego --input pod.json "data.kubernetes.admission.deny" > results.json
       if [ $(jq '.result[0].expressions[0].value | length' results.json) -gt 0 ]; then
         echo "Policy violations found:"
         jq '.result[0].expressions[0].value' results.json
         exit 1
       fi
   ```
6. **Deploy to cluster**: Apply the OPA Gatekeeper constraints via Gatekeeper's ConstraintTemplate system.

## Code Example
```javascript
# ConstraintTemplate.sample
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8ssecurity
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sSecurityConstraint
      validation: # omit for brevity
  targets:
  - target: AdmissionReview
    rego: |
      package k8ssecurity
      ...
```
```javascript
# Constraint.sample
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sSecurityConstraint
metadata:
  name: require-secure-images
spec:
  match:
    kinds: [{apiGroups: ["apps"], kinds: ["Deployment"]}]
  parameters: {registry: "registry.example.com/secure/*"}
```
```javascript
# Compliant Pod/Deployment manifest (snippet)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: compliant-app
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: registry.example.com/secure/app:1.0.0
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 1000
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8080}
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8080}
        volumeMounts: []
        resources: {requests: {cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi"}, limits: {cpu: "500m", memory: "256Mi"}}
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
```

- How would you handle legitimate exceptions or registry migrations?
